stories.headline: 2027 NFL draft questions, latest intel, risers, CFB standouts
stories.summary: How did CFB Week 10 shake up the quarterback class? CJ Carr and LaNorris Sellers rising? Here's our weekly draft spin, including top standouts.
stories.byline: Mel Kiper Jr. and Jordan Reid
stories.body:
Week 10 of the 2026 college football season was headlined by Notre Dame's big win over Miami, Oregon upsetting Ohio State, Georgia's definitive victory over Ole Miss, Utah beating BYU and Alabama making a statement against LSU. Tennessee also rolled Kentucky, and Texas topped Missouri.

What about the top 2027 NFL draft prospects? Who stood out? Yes, the draft is still about six months away, but our analysts are always looking down the road, taking early notes on top players and starting to stack their rankings for an exciting class.

With that in mind, Mel Kiper Jr. and Jordan Reid will size up college football action through a draft-centric lens on Sundays all season long. They are answering lingering questions on the best 2027 prospects, sharing insights from scouts, picking out risers to watch and pulling back the curtain on their evaluation process. Here is what they saw and heard through Week 10.

Jump to:

Week 10 | Week 9 | Week 8 | Week 7

Week 6 | Week 5 | Week 4

Week 3 | Week 2

Nov. 8

How would you restack the QB rankings after this weekend?

Reid: Week 10 was one of the more important weeks for this QB class. I'd rank the top quarterbacks as ...

Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State
CJ Carr, Notre Dame
LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina
Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss
Darian Mensah, Miami
Arch Manning, Texas

Carr was the most impressive of the bunch, finishing 29-of-40 for 319 yards and three touchdowns against Miami. He showed poise and executed timely throws. Carr's best moment of the night was a two-minute drill to close out the second quarter, when he went 6-of-7 for 79 yards and capped it off with an impressive 18-yard TD pass. Carr came in as my QB4 and certainly helped his stock ... I have him at QB2 now just behind Mestemaker.

The QB right behind Carr on the list might be the most surprising. But Sellers has made big strides in his development, and it continued against Texas A&M. Over the past five games, Sellers has 1,267 passing yards, 11 passing touchdowns and three interceptions. He has also added another 393 rushing yards and six scores on the ground. There are still a lot of highs and lows with Sellers, but the NFL is a traits-based league, and he has more than enough of them for a team to bet on him inside the top 40 picks.

After an inconsistent start to the season, Manning played his best game of the season against Mizzou. He finished 28-of-38 for 297 passing yards and three touchdowns. Manning has become more consistent with his overall execution, but his processing and timeliness in getting the ball out still need to improve.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: It seemed like Georgia running back Nate Frazier was finally back to 100 percent against Ole Miss after missing time with a rib injury and playing a bit banged-up. The 5-foot-10, 205-pound junior ran for 107 yards, showing good leg drive and rushing ability after contact. He made a nice lateral cut at one point to make a defender miss. He's a tough kid, and he doesn't just bounce everything outside like a lot of college backs -- he will run hard between the tackles and consistently pick up positive yardage.

Frazier didn't score Saturday, but he has a nose for the end zone, with 20 on the ground since 2024. Ball security was an issue early in his career, but he has cleaned that up, too. I'd like to see him get more reps catching the football -- the Bulldogs don't really use him much there -- but he has shown decent hands when given the chance. Just a solid all-around back. I have Frazier in the third or fourth round, and I think he's going to have a nice NFL career.

Reid: I mentioned him a few weeks ago, but LSU receiver Jackson Harris just keeps rising. He had 11 catches for 166 yards against Alabama. At 6-foot-2 and 202 pounds, Harris is an excellent route runner with plenty of suddenness to create easy separation. He's also competitive after the catch and can rack up yards in bunches once the ball is in his possession. Harris was already a Day 2 prospect coming into this week, and it shouldn't be out of the question that he could get into the WR3 race behind Jeremiah Smith and Charlie Becker.

Kiper: Arion Carter had a hell of a game against Kentucky. The Tennessee linebacker was all over the field. Thirteen tackles. Two sacks. Four tackles for loss. It was production in every form you want to see from a linebacker. At 6-foot-1 and 238 pounds, Carter is fast to the football, sideline to sideline; he was a track standout in high school, and you can see that speed on the tape. He diagnoses with no hesitation, reading, reacting and flying to the ball. He can drop into coverage, and he comes up in space on anything in front of him to make the tackle. And he has four sacks on the season -- he had just 1.5 in three prior years. I think Carter is just a more well-rounded player this season, and I have him in the Day 2 mix.

Reid: In a running back class that lacks much high-end talent, North Texas's Jahiem White is a late-round hopeful with 1,186 rushing yards -- currently third-most in the FBS. But it's his ability to rack up explosive plays that will make many NFL teams circle him as an intriguing target in the later rounds. The 5-foot-7, 190-pound back has 33 runs for 10-plus yards this season, including a 60-yard touchdown against Rice on Saturday.

Kiper: It has been a strong two-game stretch for North Carolina tight end Jelani Thurman. On Halloween against Miami, he caught five passes for 70 yards and two touchdowns. Then Saturday against UConn, he hauled in seven balls for 64 yard and two more scores. He is really emerging. Consider that Thurman had 13 total catches over three seasons at Ohio State (behind some really good pass catchers) before coming to UNC, and he has 45 receptions and eight touchdowns over nine games this season.

At 6-foot-6 and 245 pounds, Thurman has outstanding length, a wide catch radius, great body control and sure hands. He can reel in off-target throws and has big-play ability. Thurman also knows how to find soft spots in zone looks. His blocking has been a point of focus, and it has improved, too. Thurman has gone from off the radar to potential Round 3 target in a hurry.

Reid: With Malachi Toney out for Miami, Cooper Barkate stepped up with 10 catches for 92 yards and two scores against Notre Dame. He showed route running savvy at 6-foot-1 and 195 pounds, plus the ability to consistently beat press coverage. I have Barkate -- who joined Mensah in transferring from Duke -- with a Round 3 grade, and he's trending upward.

Kiper: Houston's Anthony Boswell just gave one of the most impressive performances I've seen from a center this season. He was key to the ground game against Cincinnati, helping the Cougars to 241 rushing yards. He drives defensive tackles off the ball, walling them off to open lanes. I don't think I saw him on the ground once. And I see good footwork and technique in pass protection. There were a few hiccups with early snaps, but it was a great day overall for Boswell.

It's a cool story here, too. Boswell was a 215-pound offensive tackle in high school and walked on at Purdue. He slowly got his weight up -- he is now 6-foot-2 and 301 pounds -- had a great 2025 season at Toledo and now is having a great campaign at Houston. He's only a third-year sophomore, and he could return to school in 2027. But I think he could be one of the top centers in this class if he declares. Bright future for the 20-year-old.

Nov. 5

Who needs to have a big game more in their much anticipated head-to-head: Darian Mensah or CJ Carr?

Reid: Carr. I've seen both of these QBs up close on the scouting trail, and they have similar traits. Mensah and Carr are both extremely smart, accurate and always in command. Scouts I've spoken to over the past month have said they each have slightly above-average physical tools, and I have them as QB3 (Mensah) and QB4 (Carr) right now.

Over the past two games, though, Carr's ball placement has been a bit off. His worst performance of the season came against BYU in Week 8, when he completed 55.1% of his passes. Even though he bounced back and completed 65.5% of his throws against Navy, he was off-target quite a bit in that game, too. Miami's pass defense has been among the worst in the country, giving up 251.9 yards per game (122nd in FBS). Carr -- who plays like a more mobile Kirk Cousins -- should be able to carve up that secondary.

Evaluators don't just need to see Carr win ... they want to see if he can be the reason the Fighting Irish win.

Which other QB are you most excited to see this weekend?

Reid: I have Ole Miss' Trinidad Chambliss vs. Georgia circled. Chambliss has had plenty of success against the Bulldogs in previous matchups. In last season's College Football Playoff, Chambliss carved up the Georgia defense, finishing with 362 passing yards and two touchdown throws.

But the speed of the Georgia defense will challenge Chambliss and his ability to play within the pocket. When he reverts to ad-libbing outside of the structure of the offense, he could face many challenges. Chambliss will be one of the more polarizing prospects in this class because of his size (6-foot, 206 pounds) and age (turning 25 before next season). Sure, those are major talking points -- but it hasn't affected his game. He remains my QB2 behind Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker.

Nov. 1

True or false: Indiana receivers Charlie Becker and Nick Marsh will both be top-20 picks.

Reid: True. Becker and Marsh are my WR2 and WR3 on my positional rankings, respectively, and both of them got in the end zone Saturday against Minnesota. Becker had eight catches for 149 yards, while Marsh had four catches for 59 yards. Becker is trending toward being a top-10 pick, and I think Marsh will clip the top 20.

Becker (6-foot-4, 208 pounds) has the speed to be a vertical threat and the body control to come down with 50-50 balls. Whenever the Hoosiers need a play, he has been their go-to target, catching a 21-yard TD pass on the very first play in overtime. And Marsh (6-3, 210) is a powerful receiver who wins with strength and competitiveness after the catch. He also isn't afraid to roll up his sleeves and do the dirty work in the box as a run blocker. On my latest board, I ranked Becker at No. 6 and Marsh at No. 18.

What is Chris Cole's best trait, and who is his best comp?

Reid: I'm not sure one trait stands out -- Cole is a true jack-of-all trades linebacker who is effective at the second level and off the edge as a blitzer and pass rusher. At 6-foot-3 and 235 pounds, he has outstanding closing speed to reach ball carriers. And in playing with an aggressive mindset, he hunts for turnovers. Cole scored on a 66-yard fumble return and finished with nine tackles and a sack against Florida on Saturday.

I see a lot of Devin Lloyd in Cole. I think Cole is an even better athlete, but he has similar shades of physicality, awareness and fast-reacting ability. I have Cole ranked No. 5 overall, and there's a Grand Canyon-sized gap between him and the next-best linebacker. Lloyd went No. 27 in 2022, but Cole has the potential to be a top-10 pick if his upward trajectory continues.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: Cal safety Kingston Lopa broke up two passes against NC State. At 6-5 and 210 pounds, the Oregon transfer can get his hands on the football, and while he didn't have any takeaways Saturday, he does have five interceptions on the season, tied for the most in the FBS. Lopa has the speed to cover a lot of ground in deep patrol over center field, but he also will step down into the box to make plays against the run. He is smooth in his back pedal, and I like his change-of-direction skills. He is my No. 3 safety; keep an eye on Lopa in the second round.

Reid: South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers has had a sudden resurgence in October. Over the past four games, he has thrown for 1,016 yards and 10 touchdowns with only three interceptions and a 64.2% completion rate. He has also added 359 yards and five touchdowns on the ground. This has also come against some good teams (Kentucky, Florida, Tennessee and Oklahoma). Saturday against the Sooners marked the second straight game in which he rushed for 96 yards and two scores.

The exciting highs and frustrating lows are still part of Sellers' game. But this surge has helped him improve from early-to-mid Day 3 to potentially Round 2.

Kiper: Clemson edge rusher Will Heldt just keeps producing. The 6-6 260-pounder has seven sacks and 11 tackles for loss over eight games, including a sack against Florida State. He got after the quarterback at Purdue before transferring to Clemson before the 2025 season, and his polished pass-rush tools are on full display every week for the Tigers. Heldt is quick to diagnose and takes good angles to the QB. And he can play standing up or with a hand down in the dirt. He's a Day 2 prospect at the moment.

Reid: In a crowded defensive tackle class, Texas Tech's A.J. Holmes Jr. has quickly ascended up the draft board. At 6-foot-3 and 300 pounds, he is an explosive wrecking ball. He has five sacks over the past three weeks and has been unblockable inside. Holmes is a quick penetrator with movement skills that few interior blockers are able to match. I'm hearing early-to-mid Day 2 grades on him, but I think he could continue to climb.

Kiper: Holmes is a powerful kid who lives behind the line of scrimmage, getting another sack against Arizona. After three seasons at Houston, he has 12 sacks with Texas Tech over the past two years. Holmes is explosive and quick. He commands double-teams inside but still works through them. He has the versatility to play a little 3-4 end, but he's really good inside.

Kiper: Oklahoma State receiver Justin Bowick is at his fourth program, going from Eastern Illinois in 2022 and '23 to Ball State in 2024 to Illinois in 2025 to Oklahoma State in 2026. It's like watching a baseball prospect move from A-ball to Double-A, Triple-A and then the majors. He caught seven passes for 124 yards and two touchdowns against Iowa State. Bowick thrives in tight coverage, and he's physical over the middle at 6-5 and 209 pounds. He has dependable hands and has averaged 17.8 yards per catch on the season. Plus, he makes an impact as a blocker. I have him in the third-round mix.

Reid: Yeah, Bowick has developed excellent chemistry with Drew Mestemaker. He is a traditional X receiver who can run past defenders and isn't afraid to make the tough catches over the middle. I have Round 4 grades on him, but as you suggested, Mel, it shouldn't come as a surprise if he rises into late-Day 2 status.

Kiper: Here's an FCS under-the-radar name for you: Montana running back Eli Gillman. He has already clipped 1,000 rushing yards, making it three straight seasons. The stats are wild over his career. Gillman has averaged 6.1 yards over 787 carries, and he just scored his 63rd and 64th rushing TDs against Eastern Washington. It also marked the fourth game this season in which he had at least one 50-plus-yard run.

Obviously, there is a lot of big-play pop to his game, but he also shows good vision, finishes his runs and has the quick feet to be elusive. And I love the energy and fire that he plays with at 6-foot, 215 pounds. Toss in great ball security, and there should be some late-Day 3 intrigue. Scouts will be looking at him. There's a lot of tread on his tires, but he has been durable. He's another FCS player -- like Rhode Island's Marquis Buchanan and Northern Arizona's Ty Pennington -- to keep an eye on.

Oct. 25

Trey'Dez Green is back. What are the chances he'll be the TE1 of the class?

Reid: I'll give it a 40% chance. Green returned after missing the previous three games with a leg injury, finishing with five catches for 50 yards and a touchdown against Auburn. He has soft hands and can attack the middle of the defense with his 6-foot-7, 237-pound frame. His run-after-catch ability is one of his best assets, too. Green's consistency as a blocker remains a work in progress, but coach Lane Kiffin has expanded his role in that area, and there's no denying that the LSU passing game builds off his alignment versatility when he mixes it up as a run blocker.

I still have Green behind Oregon's Jamari Johnson in my tight end rankings, but if he's able to remain healthy and productive during the backstretch of the season, there's a realistic chance that he could be the first tight off the board because of his diverse skill set.

What is your best comp for Dylan Stewart at the next level?

Reid: Brian Burns coming out of Florida State. He officially measured at 6-foot-5 and 249 pounds, and Stewart is listed at 6-foot-5 and 250 pounds. And their games match. The No. 3 overall player on my latest board, Stewart has exceptional bend and closing speed to constantly pressure passers, and he also understands how to utilize his length as a run defender. An argument could be made that Stewart has the highest ceiling of any defensive prospect in this class.

In his second game off suspension, Stewart made one of the biggest plays of the game, forcing a fumble to help set up the Gamecocks' upset victory over Tennessee. It was his third forced fumble in two weeks and his second straight game with a sack. Stewart will still have plenty of questions to answer throughout the predraft process -- about his overall production and the suspension from punching an Alabama player and arguing with coaches -- but there's no denying how big of an impact he has made since his return.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: Texas linebacker Rasheem Biles did a little of everything on Saturday against Ole Miss, registering four tackles (one for loss), two pass breakups and an interception. He is effective on the blitz (especially up the middle but also off the edge) and is a reliable tackler against the run. He has sideline-to-sideline range and has some impressive coverage traits for a 6-foot-1, 222-pound linebacker. Biles had at least 80 tackles over the past two seasons at Pitt before transferring to Texas, and he's off to a good start in 2026. The arrow is pointing up on the 20-year-old, and I'm thinking he could go early on Day 3.

Reid: In a thrilling Indiana-Michigan matchup, Hoosiers edge rusher Tobi Osunsanmi was arguably the best player on the field, finishing with two sacks. It was his seventh consecutive game with a sack, putting him at nine sacks for the season -- tied for second in the nation and more than he had in his past three seasons at Kansas State combined (8.5). At 6-foot-2 and 250 pounds, he's a relentless player off the edge, constantly playing with a high effort level. I have a late-Day 2 grade on Osunsanmi, but he could get into the early-Day 2 picture if his current trajectory continues.

Kiper: Speaking of Day 2 grades on Indiana players, I thought safety Amare Ferrell was great again Saturday. He added his third interception of the past two games and recorded eight tackles. On his career, Ferrell has 11 INTs -- he is always around the ball and has a knack for the big play. At 6-foot-2 and 205 pounds, he shows good awareness and instincts in coverage, and he is a solid tackler.

Kiper: Northwestern receiver Griffin Wilde had nine catches for 133 yards and a touchdown Saturday against Rutgers. Offensive coordinator Chip Kelly keeps getting the 6-2, 200-pounder the ball, and he keeps answering the bell -- Wilde has 615 yards now on the season, averaging 15.8 yards per catch. I actually remember watching him in 2024, when he was still at South Dakota State, and the Jackrabbits were playing against Oklahoma State. He went 7-150-1 that day. Wilde is a strong route runner who gets late separation and then shows good hand-eye coordination, terrific body control and a wide catch radius when the ball arrives. He can go low to secure underthrows or go up to high-point contested catches. I'd put a third- or fourth-round grade on him right now.

Reid: Linebacker Sammy Omosigho has developed into the centerpiece of the UCLA defense and has been one of the top transfers in the country (Oklahoma). At 6-2 and 239 pounds, he's instinctive and fast as a second-level defender, and he makes plenty of plays behind the line of scrimmage. He finished with six tackles and two sacks against Michigan State. I had Omosigho as my No. 3 linebacker before the weekend, but it shouldn't come as surprise if he's the second linebacker off the board behind Georgia's Chris Cole, likely in the earlier portions of Day 2.

Kiper: I love how Wisconsin edge rusher Sebastian Cheeks varies his path to the quarterback. He can get home on the inside or outside with explosion, and he always has a secondary move ready to go. We saw that against USC, with 2.5 sacks. And at 6-3 and 243 pounds, he plays with more power than you might think -- he can drive offensive tackles back with his bull rush. His motor never stops. Cheeks will make plays against the run, too, but he needs to add more weight to his frame to really take another step there. Cheeks shows sustained intensity and is a consistent player, and I have him in Round 3 or Round 4.

Reid: In a loaded wide receiver class, LSU's Jackson Harris continues to climb up my rankings at the position. The 6-foot-2, 202-pound Hawai'i transfer has established himself as a premier playmaker in Kiffin's offense, finishing with nine catches, 178 receiving yards and two touchdowns against Auburn. Harris showed his strong hands and breakaway speed on a 70-yard touchdown score. I have Harris with a Round 3 grade, but it's easy to see him rising into the top 50 picks -- or even higher.

Kiper: I'm keeping tabs on Louisiana Tech tight end Eli Finley, who had 10 catches for 128 yards and a touchdown against Old Dominion. He can be lined up inline or flexed outside, and he can block. But NFL teams are going to love targeting the 6-foot-6, 246-pounder in the red zone, too. Throw it in his area, and he will come down with it thanks to a massive catch radius. Finley is a true power forward who plays hard and fights for yards after the catch. He's an intriguing player who should test well, and while he was in the Round 5-6 range in August, I think he's already into the Round 4-5 mix.

Oct. 18

Trinidad Chambliss had yet another good game Saturday, but he lacks ideal size. Are scouts concerned about his measurables?

Reid: Well, coming into the season, scouts were pretty mixed on Chambliss' measurables -- he's listed at 6-foot and 205 pounds. Some were willing to overlook his lack of size (and the fact that he'll be a 25-year-old NFL rookie), but there was plenty of skepticism. However, in speaking to sources and NFL evaluators over the past two weeks, the consensus has gone more toward him being an exception to the rule because of his consistent ability to overcome adversity.

Chambliss is simply a gamer; nothing fazes him. He was outstanding Saturday against Missouri, throwing for 241 yards and three touchdowns while also rushing in a fourth score. Even in the Rebels' one loss to Florida, his accuracy, arm strength and mobility have shined. I still believe that Chambliss will be selected in Round 1, and more teams will see him as a blend of Bryce Young and Russell Wilson from a skill set standpoint, which can translate to the NFL.

Who impressed you most in a live viewing of Tennessee's big win over Alabama?

Reid: This was my second time seeing Tennessee defensive tackle Xavier Gilliam in person (also against Texas), and he's arguably playing like the best defender in the country. Gilliam (6-foot-2, 305 pounds) wasn't really on my radar coming into the season, but he has put himself in the mix to be one of the top defensive tackle prospects. His combination of first-step quickness, explosiveness and constant disruption reminds me a lot of Walter Nolen III, who went No. 16 overall in 2025. On Saturday, he had 0.5 tackles for loss and a pass breakup, and he recovered a fumble.

What else are you hearing this week?

Reid: Indiana's Charlie Becker continues to make a strong case for WR2 in this class (behind Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith). On Saturday against Ohio State, Becker (6-foot-4, 208 pounds) displayed a wider variety of routes in his repertoire, finishing with nine catches for 165 yards. He was primarily used as a vertical threat during the first six games of the season, but against the Buckeyes, he proved that he's a multilevel threat who can create separation on other types of routes in the intermediate areas. Becker has top-15-pick potential.

Kiper: I want to highlight another player in Indiana's losing effort -- cornerback Jamari Sharpe. He had a really good day in coverage. At 6-foot-1 and 190 pounds, Sharpe uses his length well in man-to-man coverage. But he can also play off-coverage, and when he does, he triggers really well. He can fire to the ball and is good in transition. I love how comfortable Sharpe is with his back to the QB, too. He never gets anxious and routinely turns to find the ball in time to make a play. The only time he didn't Saturday -- and really the only blemish on his outstanding day -- was on a touchdown pass where he had the WR blanketed but just didn't locate the pass. Sharpe is looking like a second-round pick.

Kiper: I thought Ole Miss running back Kewan Lacy sort of made everything go for the Rebels on Saturday against Mizzou. He turned 16 carries into 122 yards. He has the speed to get to the second level or bounce outside to the perimeter. But at 5-foot-11 and 205 pounds, Lacy is also really tough inside. He runs hard and can be creative between the tackles with subtle moves, nimble feet and physicality. I love his running style -- he just finds yards. Plus, Lacy displayed some solid pass-blocking ability (especially in the first half) and can line up out wide as a pass catcher. I have a third-round grade on him.

Reid: Houston receiver Amare Thomas made a lot of great plays against Oklahoma State, finishing with seven catches for 126 yards and two touchdowns. At 6-foot, 206 pounds, he is a sudden receiving threat who can make defenders look silly when trying to bring him down in the open field. With six touchdowns this season, Thomas is a game breaker who can change games in an instant. He got grades in the range of early-to-mid Day 3 coming into the year, but scouts that I've talked to have him graded as a top-100 prospect now.

Reid: The ascension of UCLA linebacker Sammy Omosigho continued with another standout performance against Wisconsin. The Oklahoma transfer has quickly become one of the better linebacker prospects for 2027 because of his instincts and ability to disrupt offenses -- he has five forced fumbles. Georgia's Chris Cole is the clear top linebacker in the class, but there are mixed opinions among evaluators on who's next after that. And Omosigho's effort, speed and playmaking ability make him a huge stock-up candidate with a strong Day 2 grade.

Kiper: I love's Omosigho's versatility, too. UCLA uses him both off-ball inside and off the edge outside. He can get off blocks, and he sheds and diagnoses very effectively. Omosigho is very consistent game to game.

Reid: Kentucky edge rusher Mi'Quise Humphrey-Grace now has three sacks over the past three games, including 1.5 against Oklahoma on Saturday. He's a consistent pass rusher with good hand usage. At 6-foot-4 and 271 pounds, he's able to routinely overwhelm blockers and create constant pressure throughout games. I have Humphrey-Grace with a fringe Round 3 grade, and his recent play has only helped his outlook moving forward.

Kiper: Great call, Jordan. I'm really impressed with Humphrey-Grace. But defensive tackle Tavion Gadson has also been outstanding for the Wildcats, and he also had 1.5 sacks Saturday, along with eight tackles and a pass breakup. Gadson hustles and stays active. He can navigate through multiple blockers at the snap with burst and power. And he diagnoses fast and chases well laterally. While Gadson is 6-foot-5 and 303 pounds, he moves like he's 260. He's probably a second- or third-rounder.

Reid: Tennessee safety Dejuan Lane and edge rusher Tyree Weathersby caught my eye Saturday. Lane is a Penn State transfer who has thrived in Jim Knowles' defense. At 6-foot-2 and 215 pounds, he's rangy and active on the back end but will also come down and deliver big hits against ball carriers.

At 6-foot-5 and 268 pounds, Weathersby is a major stock-up prospect after registering 5.5 sacks over the past four games, including two on Saturday. Prior to this season, he had only one career sack. Weathersby has excellent length to stay firm against the run, but he has really taken his development to another level as a pass rusher. Both Lane and Weathersby are firmly in the middle-round picture.

Oct. 11

Is Arch Manning sliding a bit in the class? Is he still an early-Round 1 prospect?

Reid: Manning has two or three plays per game that explain why some scouts still view him as a potential top-10 pick. But those plays are surrounded by too much inconsistency, which is why I have him graded as a Day 2 prospect right now on my QB Hot Board.

Manning has a curious way of making routine throws look difficult ... and difficult throws look routine. Against Oklahoma, he had a beautiful 41-yard touchdown pass to Cam Coleman in the first quarter, evading pressure and keeping his eyes downfield. But then he had two egregious fourth-quarter interceptions, one a pick-six to help the Sooners take the lead. He ultimately went 19-for-31 for 260 yards with three touchdowns and two interceptions.

At 6-foot-4 and 222 pounds, Manning has scattershot accuracy throughout games, which is a result of his footwork and mechanics being out of whack. The inconsistencies, turnovers and lack of accuracy is reminiscent of what he showed during the first half of the 2025 season.

Could LaNorris Sellers get back into the early-round mix?

Reid: Sellers entered this season as one of the most polarizing signal-callers in the class among NFL scouts and evaluators. But the past two weeks -- a combined 505 passing yards and seven total touchdowns (six passing, one rushing) against Kentucky and Florida -- have definitely been encouraging for him. On Saturday against the Gators, Sellers went 23-of-35 for 279 yards, four touchdowns and zero interceptions. He also added 20 rushing yards and a fifth score on 14 carries.

After early-season struggles with field vision and chemistry with his perimeter playmakers, Sellers has been able to piece together exciting flashes with his A-level traits. At 6-foot-3 and 238 pounds, his arm power and mobility are two of his greatest assets. Scouts whom I've spoken with view Sellers as a middle-to-late-round option. But if this current trend continues, yes, he certainly has the potential to climb back into the early-round picture. The NFL is a traits-driven league, and Sellers' arm talent could push a team to take a swing as early as near the end of Day 2.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: Charlie Becker is getting all the draft love in the Indiana wide receivers room, but don't sleep on Nick Marsh. The 6-foot-3, 210-pound target has been red-hot the past two games, going 7-120-1 against Rutgers on Oct. 3 before rolling out six catches for 187 yards and two touchdowns against Nebraska on Saturday. The Michigan State transfer mixes physicality with athleticism -- he has speed but also makes some tough tight-window catches and fights for the ball. Marsh hauled in an off-target catch Saturday, showing his improved hands this season. Marsh (who is only 20 years old) is dynamic and could make his way into the first-round conversation.

Reid: Missouri running back Jamal Roberts' draft stock is soaring right now. Taking advantage of Ahmad Hardy's absence, Roberts has made a claim as a top-five running back in this class. He finished with 222 rushing yards and two scores against Texas A&M, displaying his vision and tackle-breaking ability. At 6-foot and 216 pounds, he is a tough, rugged and grind-it-out type of runner who is challenging for defenses to bring down over the course of a game. Roberts came into the season with early-to-mid-Day 3 grades, but I think he's now a potential late-Day 2 selection.

Kiper: If you watched Oregon safety Koi Perich on Saturday against UCLA, you'd think he's a first-rounder. He's probably going to be a Day 2 pick, but there's a lot to like in his game. Perich posted 11 tackles and an interception (his second this season) against the Bruins. He reads the quarterback well and displays good range in center field. And at 6-foot-1 and 202 pounds, he's also a physical enforcer who makes plays downhill against the run. Perich is just always around the ball -- going back to his freshman year at Minnesota in 2024, when he had five INTs -- using his instincts and speed to impact all phases.

Reid: Kentucky center Coleton Price is another prospect whose stock has steadily improved over this season. In a center class that's still sorting itself out, Price is among the most consistent in the country. At 6-foot-3 and 308 pounds, he's a savvy technician with excellent hand placement. On the Wildcats' first play from scrimmage against LSU, Price paved a beautiful run lane for CJ Baxter (who turned it into a 77-yard run), showing off his powerful hands and ability to sustain at the point of attack. Price was seen as a late-round hopeful coming into the season. Now? He has a case as one of the top three players at the position. I currently have a fourth-round grade on him, and it has continued to increase over the past month.

Kiper: I think Oklahoma defensive tackle David Stone could enter the Round 1 discussion. He's a pure powerhouse, and he pushed the pocket against Texas. Centers can't handle his strength at 6-foot-3 and 312 pounds. Now, I'd like to see some more sacks on his résumé, but his on-paper stats simply don't reflect his on-field impact. Stone is super-disruptive. So while the three career sacks (including 0.5 sacks in 2026) is concerning, scouts will be intrigued by his ceiling. And he did have eight tackles for loss last season.

Staying with Oklahoma, I'll also call out Kip Lewis, the Sooners' 6-foot-1, 226-pound linebacker who is always around ball. I love his instincts and the way he shows up every week ready to compete. Lewis is a good name to watch on Day 3.

Reid: After being suspended one game following multiple incidents during the Alabama matchup on Sept. 26, South Carolina edge rusher Dylan Stewart made his return against Florida. And he got his first sack of the season, showing why he's still viewed as a potential top-10 pick. His combination of bend and closing speed are among the best in this class. Stewart will still have to answer questions about what transpired prior to his suspension -- including throwing a punch at an Alabama player and arguing with his coaches -- but his talent and overall ceiling arguably tops all defenders in the 2027 class.

Kiper: I loved watching Temple tight end Peter Clarke last season, and after a slow start to 2026, he had a big game Saturday against UConn. Clarke caught five passes for 88 yards and a touchdown. At 6-foot-6 and 265 pounds, he is a physical specimen with good hands, an impressive catch radius, some downfield ability, strong route running and after-the-catch traits. Plus, he can block, making two key ones in this game. Clarke is out of the NFL Academy in London, and he's still learning the game. He's just scratching the surface of what he can be, and I expect him to be an intriguing Day 3 pick.

Oct. 4

Is there any chance Jeremiah Smith goes No. 1 in April?

Reid: Smith will be mentioned in the same breath as some of the best receiver prospects we've ever seen, and we saw why Saturday when he caught 11 passes for 206 yards and two touchdowns against Iowa. But even elite receivers like Calvin Johnson (No. 2) and Larry Fitzgerald (No. 3) weren't selected at the top of the draft. And while I believe Smith is the unquestioned best player in the 2027 class, it's just really rare to see a wideout drafted with the top pick. That has historically been a quarterback, offensive tackle or edge rusher. And Keyshawn Johnson was the last receiver to go No. 1 -- in 1996.

There are a lot of things to consider here, though. What happens if a team that doesn't need a quarterback earns the first pick, like the Buccaneers, Chargers or Giants? Could that team trade back for a haul of selections ... or could it simply select the best player in the draft? I'll say there's a 10% chance just because Smith is that good, but I'd still project a quarterback ends up going first (even though none of the signal-callers have truly emerged quite yet).

Fill in the blank: Notre Dame will have _____ top-50 picks in April.

Reid: I think it could be as many as seven. I was in Chapel Hill to see Notre Dame up close against North Carolina this weekend, and I got to see these standouts in person.

Leonard Moore is the No. 2-ranked player on my early board; he has the length and movement skills that NFL teams covet. Quarterback CJ Carr continues to rise throughout his strong start, displaying an efficient throwing motion and good touch. He had four touchdown passes and ran in a fifth score Saturday. Edge rusher Boubacar Traore has played like a Round 1 player so far this season, finishing with six tackles and a big hit that led to an interception in the first half. Safety Brauntae Johnson didn't play Saturday, but he's No. 26 on my board. And linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa (who had an interception) and guard Anthonie Knapp should also go early.

One more name to keep an eye on: defensive end Bryce Young. He is trending upward. The 6-foot-6, 260-pounder has expanded his pass-rush repertoire and leads the team in sacks (three).

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: Yeah, Notre Dame is loaded with draft talent. I really enjoyed watching Traore on Saturday because he's not a one-dimensional edge. Yes, he has speed around the corner and the power to knock back offensive tackles in the pass rush, evidenced by 6.5 sacks last season. But he is also solid against the run and seals the edge well. Traore plays with high effort and great alertness. He's big at 6-foot-5, 253 pounds, and he could actually fill out his frame more. I have Traore in the Day 2 mix right now.

But I want to call out another Notre Dame player who probably is further down the board. Wide receiver Jordan Faison was a lacrosse player before walking onto this football team and turning his focus entirely to the sport. At 5-foot-11 and 185 pounds, he's going to be a really good slot receiver in the pros, and he's the type of kid I'd want on my team. I love his energy, toughness and overall athleticism. Against North Carolina, Faison had eight catches for 132 yards and two scores. He found himself wide open downfield on one of them, but Carr led him just a little too far; Faison tracked it, dove for it in the end zone and made a great catch. Toss in his return experience -- he has 25 career punt returns -- and Faison is a solid early-to-mid Day 3 guy.

Reid: The scorching hot start for Alabama defensive lineman Devan Thompkins -- the No. 36-ranked player on my board -- continued against Mississippi State. The transfer from USC shows an outstanding blend of size and power off the edge at 6-foot-5 and 300 pounds. And his ability is being maximized in the Alabama scheme as he moves around. He can kick inside as a 3-technique or play as a 4i-technique in a three-man defensive front. Thompkins was viewed as a fringe Day 2 prospect by NFL scouts entering the season, but he's now trending toward being a first-rounder.

Kiper: Mississippi State lost, but wide receiver Anthony Evans III popped with 12 catches for 166 yards and two touchdowns. In fact, it could have been more; Evans was wide open down the sideline on a deep ball but lost track of where he was and had a foot out of bounds. At 5-foot-11 and 190 pounds, Evans shows good hands and the ability to attack the ball in the air. He accelerates out of his cuts and breaks, and his toughness shows up when he makes catches in traffic over the middle. Just really good consistency from him. Keep an eye on him in the Day 2 range.

Reid: I'm intrigued by Missouri quarterback Austin Simmons. You might remember he started last season as the starter at Ole Miss ahead of Trinidad Chambliss. But after suffering an injury in the third game of the season, he lost the job and transferred. Saturday was only his seventh career start, but it came in a big win against a top-10 team in Florida. Simmons finished 23-of-30 for 340 yards and two TDs. He has one of the strongest arms in the country; the ball comes out of his hand with a lot of energy and velocity, and there isn't a throw he's not capable of making. Simmons (6-foot-4, 220 pounds) is a senior and still has another year of eligibility in his back pocket, so this might be more of a 2028 name. But he has my full attention.

Kiper: Ohio State left guard Luke Montgomery looks like a third- or fourth-rounder. Great tape from him against Iowa. The 6-foot-5, 313-pound senior sustained his blocks well and displayed his active hands in pass protection. His drive blocking in particular got my attention. Montgomery can make impressive pancake blocks and positional blocks. He can pull. And he can get to the second level to take on defenders.

Reid: North Carolina wide receiver Jordan Shipp (6-foot-2, 200 pounds) caught my eye while out on the scouting trail. Playing from both the slot and on the outside, he finished with seven catches for 109 yards against Notre Dame, including a nice one-handed snag against Leonard Moore. He's a name to keep an eye on throughout the season as he has turned into a go-to option for the Tar Heels. Shipp is probably a middle-round prospect right now.

Kiper: I mentioned Northern Arizona quarterback Ty Pennington in the preseason, and he has looked great in 2026. Pennington has completed at least 66% of his passes in each of his past three games, throwing six touchdown passes and one interception over that span and rushing for a seventh score. At 6-foot-2 and 220 pounds, he shows fantastic mechanics. He can move the pocket, he can make tight-window throws, and he can pick up chunks of yards with his legs. And Pennington refuses to throw interceptions -- he has just nine across 30 career starts. Pennington should get late-round consideration, and I wouldn't be surprised if he competes for a roster spot somewhere.

Sept. 27

Is Colin Simmons the runaway top edge rusher in this class?

Reid: The scouting trail continued for me this week in Knoxville, Tennessee, where I had a front-row seat for Simmons' five-sack performance against the Vols. It tied the Texas single-game record set in 1990. Outside of an excessive sack celebration from Simmons, it was one of the best defensive performances that I've ever seen. At 6-foot-3 and 246 pounds, his combination of upfield burst and closing speed make it challenging for blockers to keep pace with him. Most impressive was how many different spots he got pressure from. Simmons not only rushed from both edges but also reduced down inside on late downs and wreaked havoc from there, as well.

I got to see South Carolina's Dylan Stewart last week against Mississippi State, and he should be a top pick, too. It's likely going to be a "traits against production" debate between the two; Stewart is the more explosive athlete with better size (6-foot-5, 250 pounds), but Simmons continues to produce at an elite level (seven sacks this season). But yes ... Simmons is the clear top player at the position at this point in the season.

What's the earliest Jadan Baugh could come off the board if he keeps this up?

Reid: A tough and rugged runner at 6-foot-1 and 225 pounds, Baugh has the makings of a top-20 pick. I think the Florida standout could go in the teens, as there are a lot of NFL teams that need a true RB1.

How good has Baugh been? Per ESPN Research, he became only the second player in the past 20 seasons with at least 100 rushing yards and two rushing touchdowns in each of the first four games of a season, joining Leonard Fournette (2015). After 142 yards and three touchdowns against Ole Miss, he now has 600 rushing yards and 11 TDs on the season -- both top-two numbers in the FBS. The clear RB1 in the class so far, Baugh has terrific contact balance and lower-body quickness. With back-to-back games with at least 25 carries, he has proved that he's capable of taking on a heavy workload.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: Obviously the Dante Moore injury was the biggest news out of Oregon's win against USC, but the Ducks did get tight end Jamari Johnson back from his own injury. And that offense just looks different with him out there. Johnson caught seven passes for 119 yards. He also made a terrific one-handed catch that was called back due to a penalty.

At 6-foot-5 and 255 pounds, his game features physicality and athleticism. He has the speed to be a constant threat down the middle of the field, and he displays the hands and catch radius to haul in anything. Go back to the 2025 tape, and you'll see the ability to make defenders miss after the catch, too. His blocking is a work in progress, but he could be a first-rounder as he battles with LSU's Trey'Dez Green for the TE1 title in the class.

Reid: Georgia linebacker Chris Cole continued his tremendous start to the season. In the win against Oklahoma, he finished with eight tackles and a sack. He also had two fumble recoveries, including an 85-yard scoop-and-score. Cole's range and physicality have consistently stood out. I think his ability to diagnose and attack downhill as a run defender has improved, too. Cole is my top-ranked linebacker and is positioning himself to be a mid-to-late first-rounder.

Kiper: Cole was all over the field Saturday. He might be 6-foot-3 and 235 pounds, but he looked like a safety on those fumble returns. He is going to run really well in predraft testing. Defensive coordinators in the pros will love his ability to impact every facet of the game; he can make plays against the run, drop into coverage, or use his bend-and-burst off the edge to get home on the QB. Cole is the perfect linebacker for today's game, and his versatility allows him to play off-ball or outside. He jumps off the tape, and I love his football IQ.

But let's also give some credit to the Bulldogs' other linebacker, Raylen Wilson. He had 11 tackles and a sack Saturday. This is a dynamic duo; Cole is in the Round 1 discussion, and Wilson could go Day 2.

Reid: The draft stock of Ole Miss wide receiver Deuce Alexander continues to soar. Speaking to scouts over the summer, there were big expectations for the 6-foot, 180-pounder as he stepped into the WR1 role for the Rebels' offense. Despite a disappointing loss to Florida, he finished with seven catches for 134 yards and a touchdown. Don't be surprised to see him enter Round 1 conversations. Few other wideouts in this class offer his level of vertical speed and suddenness.

Kiper: Jordan talked about Clemson cornerback Ashton Hampton last week, and he had another big game in coverage Saturday. Playing both press and off coverage, he had three tackles and three pass breakups against Cal. Hampton crowds the receiver and gets in his hip pocket, disrupting routes right away at the line of scrimmage. He shows good recovery speed and can turn to locate the ball in coverage. And Hampton also shows the ability to plant and drive on the ball, helping him to four picks and 19 pass breakups over this career. Lockdown corner.

But how about the other Clemson corner? Elliot Washington II came over from Penn State, and he has been outstanding. He picked off two passes Saturday and has made at least one impact play in every game this season. At 5-foot-11 and 200 pounds, he is not as tall as Hampton (6-foot-2 and 205 pounds), but he has length. James Franklin used to rave about this kid. Whereas Hampton is a first-rounder, Washington probably goes on Day 2. He's a good special-teamer, too.

Reid: Tennessee defensive tackle Xavier Gilliam popped up on my radar this week (four tackles and a sack against Texas). He kept creating negative plays by getting quick penetration in the backfield. He also showed his stout presence as a run defender. The 6-foot-2, 305-pound transfer from Penn State is a name to monitor and should be added to the mix of top interior defenders in the class.

Kiper: Vanderbilt lost to Auburn, but safety CJ Heard looked good. He led Florida Atlantic in tackles in 2024 (80). He led Vandy in tackles in 2025 (71). And after nine more on Saturday, he leads the Commodores once more in 2026 (31). Heard can play centerfield or in the box because he's so quick to trigger -- he simply finds the ball. At 5-foot-11 and 210 pounds, he's compact and strong. Heard shows toughness and closing speed, and he's aggressive. I have a fourth-round grade on him, but the arrow is pointing up.

Sept. 20
Trinidad Chambliss and Darian Mensah are the current Heisman Trophy favorites. Has either QB played his way into the first round?

Reid: I do have Chambliss in Round 1 now, but I'm taking a wait-and-see approach with Mensah; Miami just hasn't played anyone yet.

Let's start with the 6-foot-3, 205-pound Mensah, whom I saw in person Friday when Miami faced Wake Forest. He started the game with an impressive 24 straight completions and finished 30-of-34 for 220 passing yards and three touchdowns. I saw real poise and command -- he seemed to be in full control of the offense during the first three quarters. I would classify his arm strength as slightly above average, as he has displayed beautiful touch down the field and enough velocity to drive the ball. The fourth quarter was the first time we saw him pressured and knocked off schedule this season, and the Hurricane's modest schedule so far brings curiosity. How will Mensah look against a higher quality opponent? Scouts already have Nov. 7 circled -- that's when Miami travels to Notre Dame. Mensah is certainly in the first-round conversation, but I want to see him against better competition.

Chambliss, meanwhile, went 33-of-48 for 363 passing yards, two passing touchdowns and one interception against LSU. Since taking over during the third game of last season, he has quickly become one of the most dynamic signal-callers in the country. His size (6-foot, 205 pounds) and age (will be a 25-year-old NFL rookie) will be major talking points, but his entire career has been about defying the odds. What gives me confidence about his next-level projection? How he elevates his play in big games and how efficiently he attacks the middle of the field. That second part is the worry with shorter passers, but Chambliss threw strike after strike Saturday night. His measurables won't be for everyone, but Russell Wilson is the NFL comparison that I use for him. If the current trend continues, I believe a team will take him in Round 1.

What is one shift on your board you didn't expect to make this early?

Reid: Charlie Becker is my new WR2. Coming into the season, I put a big grade on the Indiana receiver, ranking him as my No. 9 overall prospect. I also put him at No. 10 overall in my most recent mock draft as the third wideout off the board behind Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith and Texas' Cam Coleman. But after five catches, 127 yards and his sixth touchdown of the season against Western Kentucky, I have Becker over Coleman.

At 6-foot-4 and 208 pounds, he's a smooth vertical threat who is capable of running the full route tree. He had only eight career starts coming into the season, but he's off to a fast start. Keep in mind that he has played North Texas, Howard and WKU so far, but he produced the same results in the back end of last season and into the College Football Playoff, when he was the Hoosiers' go-to target. Becker has a knack for creating separation and rare hand-eye coordination to come down with contested catches.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: It's impressive to watch BYU running back LJ Martin run the football. He has been consistent, durable and reliable over his career, going for 1,305 yards last season, and he looked dominant on Saturday against Colorado State with 175 yards and three scores. The 6-foot-2, 225-pound back moves with power. He breaks tackles and has just enough wiggle to shake some defenders. He's a north-south rusher who can bust loose and do some damage (i.e., his 56-yard TD on Saturday). Martin is a willing blocker, too, and while he hasn't been asked to catch the football a ton, he has some receiving chops. I have Martin in the Day 2 mix right now.

Reid: South Carolina edge rusher Dylan Stewart (6-foot-5, 250 pounds) made his season debut against Mississippi State and didn't disappoint. On his very first play, he forced an errant high throw that resulted in an incompletion on third down. Stewart also had a nice run stop where he showed physicality against a puller on his way to his only tackle for loss of the game. Stewart still needs to develop countermoves, as he often got stuck if his initial plan didn't work, and he's still working his way into game shape. But overall, I thought he had a good debut and showed flashes of why many evaluators believe he has the potential to be a top-five pick.

Kiper: I recently talked about Florida State receiver Duce Robinson on the "First Draft" podcast. This kid is huge at 6-foot-6 and 230 pounds. He's in his second season with the Seminoles after transferring from USC, and he looks dynamic. He hasn't always used his frame to play like a power forward, but I saw it this weekend against Alabama. Robinson posted a 6-135-1 line, boosting his average per catch this season to 19.1 yards. He has dependable hands and can shield defenders from the ball with his body control. On his touchdown catch at the back of the end zone, he did a great job tracking the ball and getting a foot down. I see a solid Day 2 prospect.

Reid: Cal safety Kingston Lopa continued his hot start against Wagner with another interception, his fifth in three games. At 6-foot-5 and 210 pounds, he's a uniquely built safety who has flourished in his first season with the Golden Bears. He followed head coach Tosh Lupoi from Oregon to Cal, and Lopa has quickly caught my eye. Most scouts that I have talked to have late-Day 2 grades on him, and he's certainly trending upward.

Kiper: Wide receiver Chris Marshall has been all over. He started his career at Texas A&M, then went to Ole Miss. After being dismissed for a violation of team rules, he played at Kilgore College and then Boise State. Now he's with Arkansas. And the 6-foot-3, 213-pounder was great Saturday against Georgia, with seven catches for 104 yards. Marshall can make acrobatic circus catches look easy, high-pointing the ball and using his catch radius to pluck it out of the air. I had him in the later parts of Day 3 coming into the season -- and he's probably still a Day 3 guy -- but he is ascending. Keep an eye on him.

Reid: Clemson's Ashton Hampton came into the season as my third-ranked cornerback, behind only Leonard Moore (Notre Dame) and Ellis Robinson IV (Georgia) ... but he's making the CB2 race very interesting. The 6-foot-3, 205-pounder has the makings of a top-15 player. His technique and ball skills have continued to improve, and while his turnover production still needs to get better, he has constantly affected throwing windows through the first three games of the season.

Kiper: Auburn has used linebacker Xavier Atkins both off the edge and off the ball, and he just keeps making plays, with nine tackles, a sack and two tackles for loss against Florida. At 6-foot and 210 pounds, he is quick to read and react, diagnosing in an instant. But he's not just instinctive; he's also super fast to the football. That's a good combination. Atkins is in the Day 2 conversation, but he has to cut down on the missed tackles and be more aware of where the blockers are in the play. I'm going to be watching that over the rest of the season.

Reid: Through three weeks, Virginia Tech tight end Luke Reynolds is a major stock-up prospect. He already has his single-season career high for receiving yards (265). The Penn State transfer finished with 12 catches for 107 yards and a touchdown against Maryland. He's now one catch away from tying his total from all of last season (26). I think he is playing his way into Day 2 discussions, and he has an argument as TE3 right now behind Trey'Dez Green (LSU) and Jamari Johnson (Oregon).

Kiper: I wanted to see how Reynolds adjusted to the new team this season, but he is certainly moving up. At 6-foot-4 and 250 pounds, he finds soft spots in the defense and displays sure hands.

Sept. 13
Oregon's Dante Moore lost. Texas' Arch Manning pulled off a comeback. Is there any movement at the top of the QB class?

Reid: We are only two weeks into the season and there's still plenty of evaluation time left, but Week 2 spoke loudly for the top of the 2027 quarterback class. Through two weeks, Moore -- and Oregon as a whole -- has looked extremely inconsistent. He got off to a woeful start in the surprising 39-31 loss to Oklahoma State, going 1-of-6 for 9 yards in the first quarter. I saw three overthrows, and Moore didn't seem able to get comfortable. He was my top passer entering the season, but the QB1 race seems to have opened up a bit.

In fact, Manning is now my top-ranked quarterback. He led the Longhorns to 21 unanswered points in the fourth quarter in an epic 24-23 comeback win over Ohio State. He made two impressive throws in the first half that weren't even completions. He placed the ball nicely on both the bizarre interception off Cam Coleman and the clear drop by Ryan Wingo near the end zone. In the second half, Manning was 16-of-23 for 136 yards and one touchdown, and he was much more poised as he executed the offense.

Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker made a statement. In his very first game against a Power 4 opponent, he finished with 317 passing yards and two touchdowns while adding another 109 yards and a score on the ground. Mestemaker -- along with Miami's Darian Mensah -- are certainly staking their own claims in the QB1 race. But I have Manning at the moment.

Kiper: I don't know that there even is a true QB1 right now. Remember when Moore looked like Superman against Penn State last season? I keep waiting for him to show that again, but he just hasn't taken over a game since then. And while Manning led the Longhorns back, I want to see consistency across the whole game.

Mestemaker was definitely the better quarterback in that Oregon-Oklahoma State game, but he still has 17 career starts (and threw two interceptions for the second straight game). Notre Dame's CJ Carr and Miami's Mensah have looked awesome, but neither QB plays anyone of significance until they face each other ... in November (though Carr does get BYU next month). Sam Leavitt threw three interceptions for LSU against Louisiana Tech on Saturday, and NC State's CJ Bailey has had uneven play.

So far, this quarterback class -- one that was widely expected to be amazing -- has underwhelmed. There's still a lot of time. We're only through Week 2. But I want to see the group level up and play with more consistency. This is the reason I don't do rankings until October -- we have to let these guys play a bit.

Even in the loss, it was a huge game for Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith. What has impressed you most about his start to the season?

Reid: There aren't enough words to describe how special Smith is as a prospect. The most impressive part about his start is that everyone knows that the Buckeyes are going to target No. 4, and yet nobody has managed to stop him. He finished with eight catches for 164 yards and a touchdown Saturday, meaning Smith has now surpassed 150-plus receiving yards in three consecutive games dating back to last season (he had 151, plus two touchdowns, last weekend vs. Ball State). That's the longest streak for an Ohio State receiver in at least the past 30 seasons, per ESPN Research.

Smith is capable of winning with speed or power, and he's a true mismatch for any coverage that secondaries attempt to play against him. He entered the season as the top prospect overall on my board and could end up with the highest grade that I've ever given out to a receiver.

Kiper: Smith has worked on becoming more dominant after the catch, and it's showing. He can power through with his physicality, but adding that YAC fear factor could make him even more of a problem for opponents. And Smith looks quicker and more dynamic once the ball is in his hands right now.

What else are you hearing this week?

Kiper: LSU edge rusher Princewill Umanmielen had three sacks and four tackles for loss against Louisiana Tech. At 6-foot-4 and 244 pounds, he shows impressive speed off the edge and just explodes out of the blocks. But he also shows a really good inside move to beat offensive tackles and even makes plays in pursuit. I think Umanmielen could still add weight to his frame -- he gets swallowed up at times -- but he has a track record of being disruptive. He could be a good rotational pass rusher in the NFL, and I'd slot him into the second-round range right now (though he could play his way into Round 1 if he keeps this up).

Reid: The scouting trail continued for me this weekend, as I made a stop in Minnesota to see the Gophers against Mississippi State. One prospect that I wanted to pay close attention to was Bulldogs cornerback Kelley Jones. At 6-foot-4 and 205 pounds, he checks a ton of boxes for pro secondaries. His length, technique and ball skills all carried over into the game; he had a pass breakup and caused plenty of trouble for wideouts at the line of scrimmage. Jones is viewed as a potential top-40 pick, and I believe that he can end up at the back end of Round 1.

Reid: Arizona State receiver Reed Harris keeps catching my eye. The Boston College transfer finished with nine catches for 189 yards and two touchdowns against Texas A&M. At 6-foot-5 and 220 pounds, he has an outstanding frame and showcased his long speed on a 58-yard touchdown. Harris is viewed as a middle-round prospect, but with continued production, he could find himself squarely in the Day 2 mix.

Kiper: I was impressed with Harris, too. He has length and big hands, and he tracks the ball really well. He has averaged 20.7 yards per catch over his career; big plays are his calling card. And while he's being used mainly outside, I think he could be a big slot receiver at the next level. I have a similar grade on Harris at the moment, Jordan -- he's probably in that late-Day 2, early-Day 3 range.

Kiper: We weren't even sure Texas offensive tackle Trevor Goosby would be playing early in the season, with the bone bruise in his knee after an August injury in practice. But he's out there, and he played solid on Saturday night against the Buckeyes. Goosby anchors well, making him tough to beat in pass protection. But despite not being the most athletic OT prospect, he also made a nice block in space. The 6-foot-7, 325-pounder remains very consistent, and he's a clear early-to-mid Round 1 guy.

Reid: Michigan edge rusher John Henry Daley was a major addition in the transfer portal for the Wolverines, and he showed why in the 17-10 upset victory over Oklahoma. At 6-foot-5 and 252 pounds, he finished with a sack and three tackles for loss, as his tenacious effort and deep repertoire of pass-rush moves were on full display. Daley suffered a torn Achilles last November while at Utah, and there were question marks about his overall explosiveness post-injury, but he has shown why many scouts believe he's a top-100 prospect with the potential to climb even higher.

Kiper: Alabama's Devan Thompkins is going to have a lot of NFL eyes on him this fall if he keeps playing this way. At 6-foot-5 and 300 pounds, he is probably a 3-4 defensive end in the pros. He can win off the edge, he can win with a rip move, and he can win with his bull rush. Despite his size, he can even drop into coverage, and he made a nice play there against Kentucky. Thompkins brings scheme versatility, and you'll see him move inside at times. But no matter where he lines up, he brings imposing size at the point of attack and plays with high intensity. Thompkins had two sacks Saturday. He's a second-round player with the potential to rise.

Kiper: I think Missouri quarterback Austin Simmons might be a 2028 guy because he has started only four games, but he has looked good so far this season. The Ole Miss transfer can spin it with the best of them, and the ball jumps out of the lefty's hand. He throws with accuracy and touch -- he's a pure passer. After three TD passes against Kansas on Friday night, he has a spotless 7-0 touchdown-to-interception ratio on the season.

stories.headline: Man United go 2-0 down in four minutes, fastest in club's Premier League history
stories.summary: Manchester United conceded two goals against Aston Villa on Sunday in just three minutes and 42 seconds, the earliest they have ever been 2-0 down in a Premier League game.
stories.body:
Manchester United conceded two goals against Aston Villa on Sunday in just three minutes and 42 seconds, the earliest they have ever been 2-0 down in a Premier League game.

Nicolas Jackson pounced on a spill by Senne Lammens after the Belgian goalkeeper had spilled a shot by Alysson to turn the ball home, doubling Villa's advantage after the Brazilian had opened the scoring in the first minute.

Villa's 2-0 lead is the second-earliest in the Premier League this season, only behind Chelsea's fast start against Bournemouth, in which they had a two-goal advantage after two minutes and 29 seconds.

It is also the first time since a game against Nottingham Forest in August 2023 that United have conceded two goals in the opening five minutes of a Premier League match at Old Trafford. United went on to win that match 3-2.

United began the game in the relegation zone for the first time in 40 years after Nottingham Forest beat Manchester City on Saturday.

Michael Carrick's side are in crisis, having not won a league game since August -- a 5-2 victory against Ipswich Town which remains their only Premier League victory this season.

United fans, who had already protested against the club's owners ahead of the match, chanted "We want Glazers out!" after Jackson doubled Villa's advantage.

What you need to know for Sunday

Doncic, if you haven't heard, is on quite the scoring bender to open the season, averaging 40.1 points while topping Michael Jordan for the most points through eight games since the merger. If Doncic were to sit, Austin Reaves becomes a building block in DFS lineups and for offensive props.

The Pistons feature fellow MVP candidate Cade Cunningham, although defensive force Ausar Thompson might prove just as critical guarding Doncic and Reaves throughout the game. Even just 10% into the season, this should be a revealing matchup for both teams.

The slate opens with a Midwest matinee as the Philadelphia 76ers visit the Chicago Bulls. Joel Embiid is listed as probable for Philadelphia, while Chicago could be without frontcourt contributors Nic Claxton and Zach Collins. The 76ers are nearly double-digit favorites, part of a larger trend today, as four of the seven games have spreads of at least 9.5 points.

This makes today's closer lines, particularly the Lakers visiting Detroit (-4.5), the Dallas Mavericks (-7.5) against the Brooklyn Nets, and the Pelicans taking on the Clippers (-1.5), especially interesting for the predictability of playing time and workloads in each rotation.

stories.headline: Pedro Martinez appeals for MLB resolution, reflects on effects of 1994 strike
stories.summary: Pedro Martinez appealed to both MLB players and owners to find a solution to their CBA talks, saying "get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."
stories.body:
Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martinez spoke out about the looming lockout hanging over Major League Baseball, saying a resolution must be found to protect the sport and fans.

"I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," Martinez said Saturday, according to the Boston Herald. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."

In Boston for the Pedro Martinez Foundation's 10th annual gala, Martinez said that "honestly speaking, I'm pissed" as he appealed to both players and owners to find a solution.

"Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball," Martinez said.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. MLB owners are trying to put a salary cap in place. Their latest offer, made Tuesday, would delay the implementation of the cap until 2028.

The players' union has remained steadfast against any talks of a salary cap during negotiations.

Martinez was hurt in multiple ways by a previous baseball stoppage early in his career. At the time of the 1994 strike, he was in his first season with the Montreal Expos, who had the best record in the majors at 74-40 and dreams of a World Series title when play was stopped. The cancellation of the rest of the 1994 season also kept Martinez a day away from arbitration eligibility.

"I hope the commissioner can see me and hear and the players' association hears what I have to say. I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before," Martinez said. "... I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money. So I hope they don't mess it up and they don't mistreat the fans."

"Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better. This time, there's no excuse," Martinez added in comparing the 1994 strike to today. "On both sides, not the PA, not the owners, not baseball. The fans do not deserve to be mistreated."

Martinez was a three-time Cy Young Award winner and eight-time All-Star who won the 2004 World Series with the Boston Red Sox and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2015.

stories.headline: Conor McGregor insists it has to be Max Holloway for final UFC fight
stories.summary: Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.
stories.body:
Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.

Back in July, Holloway (28-9) defeated McGregor (22-7) via TKO in just 69 seconds, after McGregor injured his right knee in the opening seconds of their welterweight bout in Las Vegas.

Speaking at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight news conference on Saturday, McGregor, 38, once again reiterated his desire to run it back with Holloway.

"It has to be Holloway," McGregor told reporters.

"Just do the f------ thing again. Just do the thing again. The guy didn't engage once. He's the one that called for the stoppage in the fight. He said 'ref, ref!'

"He's the one stopping the fight. Imagine I just said 'yay!' and jumped the fence. I won! He doesn't want to f------ fight.

"On the one leg, he wasn't coming near me. It's so shocking and so heartbreaking to me and I'm still f------ dealing with it. It has to be Holloway. Just f------ dust it off, re-do it."

On the rehab, McGregor stated he's looking for a return potentially before the summer next year and also hinted if Holloway isn't available he could look elsewhere for an opponent.

"I'm on my way back," McGregor said.

"What's it now November? Three months I'm off of surgery. I done this injury before and returned within nine months. So nine months is pre-summer. I just want to go again and again."

"Something might happen, I don't know. But a fighter that fights me, put some respect on my name. If you're not a world champion fighter, if you've not got world accolades to your name, don't utter my f------ name."

The fight against Holloway at UFC 329 was McGregor's first appearance since July 2021 and he has now suffered serious lower-body injuries in each of past two fights, including a fractured leg against Dustin Poirier in 2021.

stories.headline: Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer set for spell on sidelines with foot injury
stories.summary: Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.

Neuer had to go off with the injury shortly before halftime in Bayern's 2-1 Bundesliga win at Mainz on Saturday.

Bayern's statement did not give a specific length of layoff for the German goalkeeper, only stating it would be 'for the time being'.

"Manuel Neuer will be out of action for FC Bayern for the time being," the club said.

"The captain sustained a partial tendor tear in his right foot during the German record champions' 2-1 win against 1.FSV Mainz 05 on Saturday, as confirmed by an examination by the FC Bayern medical unit.

"Neuer was substitued shortly before half-time at Mainz."

Replacement goalkeeper Jonas Urbig filled in, as he has often done for the veteran Neuer this season. Urbig is viewed as Neuer's long-term successor at the club and the injury presents a chance to demonstrate he can eventually take the role.

The injury is another blow to Bayern's season following Vincent Kompany's battles with issues that saw him collapse at training. He was hospitalised and treated for meningeal irritation, which is an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord.

Neuer has only made five league appearances this season, while the 23-year-old Urbig has also made five, including his substitute appearance Saturday.

It was a bittersweet moment for Neuer as he also became Bayern's oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days old in the game.
